newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Serbia's 1996 sugar output seen around 270,000 T.
newsitem.headline: Serbia's 1996 sugar output seen around 270,000 T.

text.p: Serbian sugar refineries could process about 2.5 million tonnes of sugar beet and produce around 270,000 tonnes of sugar this season, an industry expert said on Wednesday.
"We can produce up to 280,000 tonnes of sugar this season and cover domestic needs," Milan Petrovic, director of one of the top Serbian sugar refineries in Crvenka, said.
According to other expert estimates, Serbia's sugar needs run between 350,000 and 400,000 tonnes a year.
"The average expected sugar content in this season's sugar beet crop was around 15.5 percent against 14 percent in the previous season," Petrovic told Reuters.
The government plans to raise the area under sugar beet by 30,000 hectares in 1997, taking it to 110,000 hectares, said Vlajko Stojiljkovic, head of the Serbian Chamber of Commerce.
The state's aim was to boost sugar production to 700,000 tonnes in 1997, equivalent to the refineries' capacity.

Petrovic said this figure was unrealistic, but even if the increased crop managed to produce a surplus over domestic consumption, he insisted there would be no exports until the state met producers' demands.
"As long as the government does not provide export subsidies, we cannot sell abroad, because we'll have to export at lower prices," he said.
The refinery director added that the main bottlenecks lay with inefficient agriculture, difficulties with weeding and inadequate infrastructure.
Sugar refineries were seeking new price parities from the government, intervention by the Commodity Reserve Agency and protection from substantially cheaper imports.

According to Petrovic, the production cost for locally refined sugar was 4.68 dinars (1.47 German marks) per kg -- well above the retail price of 3.95 dinars. One kg of imported Cuban sugar does not exceed 1.4 marks, he said.

Producers are demanding protection from cheaper imports, which totalled about 100,000 tonnes of raw sugar and 40,000 tonnes of white sugar during January-August. The most efficient protection would be introducing import quotas, he said.
Under the Yugoslav system, refineries are responsible for organising farmers to grow enough sugar beet for their needs. Refineries are prohibited from buying beet on the open market.
Farmers are reluctant to grow sugar beet because cash payments cover only one third of the crop's value. The balance is paid in fuel and fertilisers.
The government pays farmers a maximum of 0.27 dinars per kg of sugar beet.
